title: The Last Big Performance
subtitle: Lanternweald — sixth expansion pass
content:
The invitation was written in letters three inches high.

MAUI, HERO OF THE TIDE, WILL OPEN THE REPAIR CELEBRATION.

He stared at the poster with an expression I couldn't read.

"Well," I said.

"Well."

I waited for him to lift his chin and begin planning a speech about himself.

Instead he asked, "Who decided that?"

Pip appeared from behind the lantern table.

"The entertainment committee. They thought people would like something exciting after all the repairs."

Maui looked around the square.

His grin flickered over the poster. For a breath I saw the old hunger in his face: the gigantic letters, the crowd calling his name, everybody waiting to see what he would do.

Mini Maui struck a heroic pose on his chest and began counting imaginary cheers.

Maui covered him with one hand.

"Okay," he muttered. "I am not going to pretend this isn't flattering."

Pip raised an eyebrow. "But?"

"But somebody's got to carry the benches, the kids have their show, and I am fairly certain Fen will throw me into the sea if I set off fireworks near the rigging."

"You could still introduce the event," I said.

Maui considered it. "I could. With a dramatic speech, a magnificent transformation, perhaps an interpretive dance—"

"No fireworks," Pip interrupted.

"Your people are relentless."

He laughed, and I loved that he could admit wanting the spotlight without making it the condition for helping. He was still a demigod who liked to hear his own name. The difference was that he could let other names be said beside it.

"Tell me where the benches go," he said. "Then we'll talk about the interpretive dance."

The temporary surface channel had passed its second inspection. Riverstone's bridge was almost ready for its final load test. The western Starwake boards had reopened, and the Brasswatch generator had stopped behaving like an offended dragon. The village had survived a string of storms and repairs, but the lower service passage remained closed while engineers studied its age and the old decisions surrounding it.

There was reason to celebrate.

There was also a lot of work that didn't belong to one famous man.

"I don't want to be the opening act," Maui said.

Pip blinked.

"You don't?"

"No."

"Are you sure?"

He looked at me.

I didn't answer for him.

"Yes," he said.

The disappointment was real. I could see it cross Pip's face. They had hoped for a draw, something that would make the square full and the donation box heavier.

Maui noticed.

"I can help with something else," he offered. "If you need it."

Pip looked toward the pile of lantern hooks.

"Actually..."

We spent the next two days preparing the celebration.

Greg would play a short original set, because he had chosen to and could leave when it was over. The children from Tidewake wanted to perform their little story about Fen falling into the harbor. Fen protested until they discovered they had been given the role of the wise crab.

Iroh offered tea. Mara brought bread. Tamsin made sure the decorations were mounted on independent supports rather than the ancient arches. Edda checked the viewing areas so people could sit or stand without blocking the routes.

Maui helped Pip sort hooks.

It was possibly the least glamorous work he'd ever done.

He was very bad at sorting.

"Those are the long ones," Pip told him.

"They look short."

"Compared with your hand, everything looks short."

I laughed from the next table.

Maui held up a hook.

"This one?"

"Medium."

He sighed.

"How can there be so many kinds of hook?"

"How can there be so many kinds of fish?" Pip asked.

He considered.

"Excellent point."

On the evening before the festival, the volunteers met to confirm what the celebration actually required. Pip had written a cheerful program, but the schedule had no break between the children's kite display and the lantern procession. Greg was listed for three songs despite having agreed to two.

"He'll still do three," somebody said. "He likes playing."

"Ask him," I said.

We found Greg sorting cables by the stage. He was happy to play two. The third song wasn't ready, and he'd promised to be back in Beach City the next morning. Nobody was entitled to turn a friendly offer into an obligation.

Pip revised the program without grumbling. The children chose a shorter kite demonstration because Fen had posted an afternoon wind warning. Tamsin checked that the lantern stands could be moved without blocking Edda's turning space. Mara counted the bread orders against the bakery's actual flour supply.

Maui carried chairs while we worked. When one volunteer asked whether he could still give a short heroic introduction, he stopped and looked at the children waiting to test their lantern hooks.

"I'd rather introduce the people who did the repairs," he said. "If they want to speak."

Several of them didn't. The council decided a name could go on the public thanks list only with permission; private volunteers could be thanked collectively. One worker asked not to be identified at all. Pip crossed the name out without asking why.

Later Maui admitted that he'd imagined the crowd chanting for him.

"You can want applause," I said. "You just can't collect it on someone else's behalf."

"I know. I just really wanted them to chant my name. In rhythm. Then I felt like an idiot for wanting it."

"It doesn't. You look ridiculous when you try to hide behind a basket of lantern hooks."

He peered over the basket. "Then my disguise has failed."

I laughed and kissed him on the cheek. There was no grand lesson written on the program, only accurate times, safe paths, and people who'd agreed to be there.

Pip brought the revised poster round after sunset, its corners curling where the ink was still wet.

"Could you look before I hang it?" they asked Maui.

He held it at arm's length. The words were smaller than before. The children's performance sat at the top, followed by the inspection-fund supper and the lantern walk. No one's name occupied half the paper.

Maui swallowed.

"Are you disappointed?" Pip asked.

He took much too long to answer. "A little."

Pip's mouth tightened. I thought they might apologize, though they hadn't done anything wrong.

"I used to like seeing my name," Maui said. "That isn't your responsibility."

"It's okay to have a name on the poster," Pip replied. "You were helping with the benches."

He looked down at the volunteer list, where his name stood between Lio and Edda. "It seems very small."

"So is mine," Pip said. "I painted six of them."

That made him laugh. Pip did not join in until he stopped. Then they asked whether he would carry the sign to the square, because the paint was wet and he had steady hands.

I watched him take it carefully by the wooden frame instead of holding it over his head like a victory banner.

Later, while we walked through the lantern-lit market, Maui caught my sleeve.

"I know you love other people," he said. "I know I'm not supposed to turn this into a competition. But I miss being somebody everyone looks for."

"Do you want me to pretend I don't see you?"

"No." He rubbed the back of his neck. "I want you to notice the parts nobody else looks for."

I thought of the way he'd carried the poster so Pip's paint wouldn't smudge. Of his quiet face when a child asked a question he couldn't answer. I told him both.

His smile arrived slowly, uncertain at the edges.

"That feels different," he said.

"It is."

He leaned close, then hesitated because people were walking past with armfuls of chairs. I pulled him aside by the lantern shed and kissed him, deliberately and a little awkwardly, with the smell of wet paint still on his hands. We laughed when a hook rattled above us. He didn't ask whether anyone had seen.

By festival morning, the poster had been replaced. It listed the schedule without turning any person into the center of the world. Maui's name appeared under *volunteer setup*, alongside Pip, Lio, Edda, and a dozen others.

He looked at it for a long moment.

"Do you regret it?" I asked.

"Some of it."

I nodded.

"Which part?"

"I like being seen."

"I know."

"I think I always will."

"That's not a crime."

He looked relieved.

"I just don't want to need it to know who I am."

We stood together beneath the lanterns.

Then Lio shouted for help with the stage ramp, and Maui went to ask what they needed.

The celebration began late because the first tray of bread had to be rescued from an overenthusiastic oven. Nobody minded. Aang helped the children launch a few kites from the safe ridge, keeping sacred Air Nomad traditions separate from a local craft festival. Toph called the whole event "terribly sentimental" and then refused to leave before the last performance.

Greg played a song about a ferry bell.

It was quieter than the crowd expected.

People listened.

I saw Maui standing at the edge of the square, holding a spare lantern pole in one hand. He wasn't watching the stage. He was watching a child who couldn't quite reach the hook they'd been assigned.

He knelt, held the pole steady, and asked whether they wanted help.

The child nodded.

Together they hung the lantern.

No applause.

No one even turned to look.

Something in my chest ached.

Later, when the crowd began moving toward the food stalls, Maui came to find me.

"Did I miss anything?"

"The wise crab was excellent."

"Naturally."

"Greg played beautifully."

"I heard."

"And you helped Pip."

He shrugged.

I stepped closer.

"I saw you with the lantern."

His eyes widened.

"You did?"

"Yes."

He looked almost shy.

"Was it all right?"

"It was lovely."

He let out a breath.

I took his hand and pulled him behind the sheltered garden wall, out of the flow of people. The lanterns made soft gold patterns on the stone.

"Can I kiss you?" I asked.

His smile was sudden and warm.

"Please."

I kissed him. His hands settled carefully at my waist, and for a few moments the festival noise became a distant, pleasant blur. We laughed against each other when a paper fish caught in his hair.

"Your audience has arrived," I whispered.

"A terrible critic."

"Very."

We rejoined the crowd after the lantern keeper checked the final hooks. The donation box held enough to fund part of the next inspection, and the public ledger recorded the amount. No one promised the service tunnel would reopen because the celebration had gone well.

At the end, Pip thanked the volunteers.

Maui was named with everyone else.

He clapped for the children.

When we walked home, he carried no trophy.

Only a small bent hook he'd rescued from the sorting pile, because he thought we could use it in the garden.

We couldn't.

I let him keep it anyway.
